title: The present tense: regular verbs
summary: Regular verbs drop -ar, -er or -ir and add an ending for each person. One pattern covers most of the verbs you'll meet.

rules.rule: Yo, tú, él, ella, usted, nosotros, ellos, ellas, ustedes
Usted and ustedes take the él and ellos forms
rules.note: Ustedes is the plural you everywhere in Latin America, for friends and strangers alike.

rules.rule: The pronoun is often left out, since the ending already says who
Drop -ar and add -o, -as, -a, -amos, -an

examples.es: Hablo con mi mamá todos los días.
examples.en: I talk to my mom every day.
My aunt and uncle speak English.

sections.heading: -er and -ir verbs, like comer and vivir

rules.rule: -er verbs add -o, -es, -e, -emos, -en
-ir verbs add the same endings, except -imos for nosotros

examples.en: They write a lot of messages.

rules.note: Only the nosotros form tells -er and -ir verbs apart: comemos, vivimos.

rules.rule: What happens regularly, or is true now
What's happening right now, where English uses -ing

examples.en: "What are you looking for?" "I'm looking for my keys."

rules.rule: Plans for soon, with a time word
No goes right before the verb
rules.note: There's no word for do or does: the verb itself is negative or asks the question.

rules.rule: A yes or no question is the same sentence with ¿ and ?
Question words come first and have a written accent

title: The present: stem changes and irregular yo forms
summary: Many common verbs change a vowel in their stem, and some have a yo form of their own. The endings stay regular.

rules.rule: e becomes ie: pensar, querer, empezar, cerrar, preferir, entender

examples.es: La clase empieza a las ocho.

rules.rule: o becomes ue: poder, volver, dormir, encontrar, contar, almorzar

examples.es: Mis padres vuelven a las seis.
examples.en: My parents come back at six.

rules.rule: e becomes i, only in -ir verbs: pedir, servir, repetir, seguir
Jugar is the only u that becomes ue
rules.note: Jugar fútbol is usual in much of Latin America, and jugar al fútbol is also correct.

rules.rule: Nosotros keeps the original vowel

examples.en: We want to go to the movies.

rules.note: The forms that change make a boot shape in the verb table: yo, tú, él and ellos, but not nosotros.

rules.rule: A -go ending: hacer, poner, salir, traer, oír

examples.es: Hago la tarea después de cenar.
examples.en: I do my homework after dinner.

examples.es: Salgo de casa a las siete.

rules.note: Only yo changes: haces, hace, hacemos, hacen.

rules.rule: A -zco ending: conocer, and most verbs ending in a vowel plus -cer or -cir
Others of their own: sé, veo, doy

examples.es: Veo a mis abuelos los domingos.
examples.en: I see my grandparents on Sundays.

rules.rule: Tener, venir and decir: an irregular yo form and a stem change

examples.es: Vengo mañana, y ellos vienen hoy.
examples.en: I'm coming tomorrow, and they're coming today.

examples.es: Yo digo que sí y ella dice que no.
examples.en: I say yes and she says no.

rules.rule: The most common verbs are irregular in every form

examples.es: Voy a la escuela en bus.
examples.en: I go to school by bus.

rules.note: Ir: voy, vas, va, vamos, van. Ser: soy, eres, es, somos, son. Estar: estoy, estás, está, estamos, están.

title: Gustar and verbs like it
summary: Me gusta works the other way around from English: the thing you like is the subject, and a pronoun says who likes it.

rules.rule: Gusta for one thing, gustan for more than one
rules.note: Literally, coffee pleases me. The verb agrees with the coffee or the dogs, not with you.

rules.rule: With an infinitive, always gusta
The pronoun says who likes it: me, te, le, nos, les

examples.es: Nos gustan las películas de terror.

examples.en: Do you all like the beach?

sections.heading: Making it clear, or stressing it

rules.rule: A plus a name or pronoun says who le or les means

examples.es: A Ana le gusta el chocolate.
A mis padres les gusta viajar.

rules.note: The pronoun stays: a Ana le gusta, never a Ana gusta.

rules.rule: A mí and a ti add stress or contrast

examples.es: A mí me gusta, pero a ti no.
examples.en: I like it, but you don't.

rules.rule: Agreeing: a mí también, and a mí tampoco after a negative

examples.es: —No me gusta el frío. —A mí tampoco.

sections.heading: Verbs that work the same way

rules.rule: Encantar: to love something
rules.note: Encantar is already strong, so it doesn't take mucho.

rules.rule: Interesar, importar, molestar
Faltar: to be missing, or still to go

examples.es: Faltan dos días para mi cumpleaños.
examples.en: My birthday is two days away.

rules.rule: Doler: to hurt
rules.note: Body parts take el or la, not mi: me duele la cabeza.

rules.rule: Parecer, for opinions
The pattern stays the same

examples.es: De niño me gustaban los dulces.
examples.en: As a kid I liked candy.

title: Nouns, articles and adjectives
summary: Every noun is masculine or feminine, and the words around it, like the, a, this, my and its adjectives, change to match.

sections.heading: Every noun is masculine or feminine

rules.rule: Most nouns ending in -o are masculine, and most ending in -a are feminine
Some common ones break the pattern
rules.note: Learn each noun with its article. The guide to noun gender and plurals has more patterns and exceptions.

rules.rule: Nouns for people often have both forms
The: el, la, los, las
A and some: un, una, unos, unas

examples.en: I'm looking for a big house.

rules.rule: A and el join as al, and de and el join as del
rules.note: Only with el: a la playa and de la casa stay as they are.

rules.rule: Spanish uses the where English doesn't
rules.note: And the other way around: no un with a profession. Soy maestra means I'm a teacher.

rules.rule: Add -s after a vowel and -es after a consonant
A final z becomes c
A mixed group takes the masculine
Adjectives ending in -o have four forms

examples.es: un carro rojo, una casa roja
examples.en: a red car, a red house

examples.es: unos carros rojos, unas casas rojas
examples.en: some red cars, some red houses

rules.rule: Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant only change for the plural

examples.es: un examen fácil, una pregunta fácil
examples.en: an easy test, an easy question

rules.rule: Nationalities and words ending in -or add -a

examples.es: un chico español, una chica española
examples.en: a Spanish boy, a Spanish girl

rules.rule: Usually after the noun
Numbers and words for how many go before
Bueno and malo drop the -o before a masculine noun, and grande becomes gran
rules.note: Gran before a noun means great, and grande after it means big: un gran hombre, un hombre grande.

rules.rule: Mi, tu and su add -s for a plural noun
Nuestro agrees like any adjective ending in -o
Su can mean his, her, its, their or your

examples.en: His, her, their or your house is big.

examples.es: La casa de ella es grande.

rules.note: When it isn't clear, say de él, de ella, de ellos or de usted after the noun.

rules.rule: Este for this, ese for that, aquel for that over there
On their own, they mean this one or that one

examples.en: Which do you prefer, this one or that one?

rules.rule: Esto and eso for ideas, or things you can't name

title: Ser vs. estar
summary: Both mean "to be". Ser says what something is; estar says how or where it is right now.

rules.rule: Identity, profession and origin
Traits that describe what something is like
Time, dates and possession

examples.es: El carro es de mi tío.

rules.rule: Where an event takes place

examples.es: La fiesta es en mi casa.
examples.en: The party is at my house.

rules.rule: Location of people and things
rules.note: Even permanent locations take estar.

rules.rule: Temporary states, moods and conditions
Actions in progress, with the gerund
Aburrido: boring with ser, bored with estar
Listo: clever with ser, ready with estar
Rico: wealthy with ser, delicious with estar
Malo: bad with ser, sick or gone off with estar
Muerto takes estar, even though death is permanent
Casado usually takes estar in everyday speech
Contento always takes estar, but feliz can take either
rules.note: Textbooks teach ser with feliz, but estar feliz is very common in Latin America, especially for happiness about something right now.

title: Por vs. para: the basics
summary: Both can mean for. Para points toward a goal: a purpose, a person, a place or a deadline. Por is about the reason behind something, or the way through it.

rules.rule: Purpose: in order to
Who something is for
Where someone is headed
A deadline

examples.es: La tarea es para el lunes.

rules.rule: In someone's opinion

examples.es: Para mí, el español es fácil.

sections.heading: Por: why, which way, and how

rules.rule: The cause or reason

examples.es: Siempre llego tarde por el tráfico.
examples.en: I'm always late because of the traffic.

rules.note: Gracias always takes por, because you're thanking someone for a reason.

rules.rule: Through or along a place
A price or exchange

examples.es: Pago diez dólares por la camisa.
examples.en: I'm paying ten dollars for the shirt.

rules.rule: How you get in touch

examples.en: I'll call you on the phone.

rules.rule: Parts of the day
rules.note: With a clock time it's de: a las ocho de la mañana.

rules.rule: Worth learning whole
¿Por qué? asks why, and porque answers

examples.en: "Why are you studying Spanish?" "Because I like it."

rules.rule: A goal or destination takes para, and a reason or route takes por

examples.en: I'm buying flowers for my mom.
I'm here because of my mom.

rules.note: The flowers go to her, so para. She's the reason you're here, so por. The full guide to por and para has more uses.

title: Por vs. para
summary: Para points toward a goal or destination. Por looks back at a cause, or covers a route, exchange or length of time.

rules.rule: Purpose: in order to

examples.en: I study in order to learn.

rules.rule: Recipient
Destination
Deadline

examples.es: La tarea es para el lunes.

rules.rule: Opinion and comparison

examples.es: Para su edad, es muy alto.
examples.en: For his age, he's very tall.

rules.rule: Cause or reason

examples.en: I was late because of the traffic.

rules.rule: Movement through or along
Exchange or price

examples.es: Pagué diez dólares por la camisa.
examples.en: I paid ten dollars for the shirt.

rules.rule: Duration

examples.en: I lived there for five years.

rules.rule: Means of communication or transport

examples.en: I'll call you on the phone.

rules.rule: On behalf of

examples.en: I did it for my mother's sake.

rules.rule: Agent in the passive voice

examples.es: La casa fue construida por mi abuelo.
examples.en: The house was built by my grandfather.

rules.rule: These are worth memorizing as units
The choice can change what you're saying

examples.en: I work for my uncle (he's my boss).
I'm working in my uncle's place.

title: The preterite: regular verbs
summary: The preterite tells what happened and was finished. Regular verbs have one set of endings for -ar and another shared by -er and -ir.

rules.rule: -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -aron

examples.en: Did you talk to your boss?

examples.es: El presidente habló en la radio.
examples.en: The president spoke on the radio.

rules.note: The accent matters: hablo is I speak, habló is he spoke.

rules.rule: -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -ieron

sections.heading: Nosotros, the same as the present

rules.rule: -ar and -ir verbs use one nosotros form for both tenses

examples.en: Last night we went out late.

rules.note: A time word usually makes it clear. -er verbs differ: comemos, comimos.

rules.rule: In the yo form, -car becomes -qué, -gar becomes -gué and -zar becomes -cé
rules.note: Only the spelling changes, to keep the sound. The other forms are regular: buscaste, llegó, empezamos.

rules.rule: An i between two vowels becomes y: leer, creer

examples.es: Leyó el libro en un día.
examples.en: She read the book in a day.

rules.rule: Present stem changes don't carry over in -ar and -er verbs

examples.es: Volví a casa a las diez.
examples.en: I came back home at ten.

rules.note: -ir verbs like pedir and dormir do change, in the él and ellos forms. They're in the guide to irregular preterites.

rules.rule: Finished actions, often with a time word

examples.es: La semana pasada viajamos a Quito.
examples.en: Last week we traveled to Quito.

rules.rule: One event after another
Recent events too, in Latin America
rules.note: Where Spain often says he comido, Latin America usually says comí.

title: The preterite: irregular verbs
summary: The most common verbs have their own preterite stems, with endings that have no written accents. Some -ir verbs change a vowel instead.

sections.heading: Ser and ir share one preterite

rules.rule: Fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fueron
rules.note: The sentence tells them apart: fue al cine is went, fue difícil is was.

rules.rule: The endings are -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron, with no written accents
Stems with u: tener tuv-, estar estuv-, poder pud-, poner pus-, saber sup-

examples.en: We were in Cartagena for a week.
Where did you put the keys?
I found out the news yesterday.

rules.rule: Stems with i: hacer hic-, querer quis-, venir vin-

examples.es: Mis primos vinieron a la fiesta.
examples.en: My cousins came to the party.

rules.note: Hacer writes hizo, with z, to keep the sound.

rules.rule: Stems with j: decir dij-, traer traj-, conducir conduj-
rules.note: The ellos ending drops its i: dijeron, trajeron.

rules.rule: Dar takes -er endings, and neither needs a written accent

examples.es: Le di un regalo a mi mamá.
examples.en: I gave my mom a present.

rules.rule: Hubo for something that happened

examples.es: Hubo un accidente en la carretera.
examples.en: There was an accident on the highway.

rules.note: It's always singular, and for a description you use había: había mucha gente.

rules.rule: e becomes i in the él and ellos forms: pedir, servir, repetir, seguir, sentir, preferir
rules.note: The other forms are regular: pedí, pediste, pedimos.

rules.rule: o becomes u in the same forms: dormir, morir

title: The imperfect
summary: The imperfect describes the past as it was going on: habits, descriptions and the background to events. Only three verbs are irregular.

rules.rule: -ar verbs: -aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -aban

examples.es: Mi papá trabajaba en un banco.
examples.en: My dad worked at a bank.
We used to walk to school.

rules.rule: -er and -ir verbs: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían

examples.en: I used to eat a lot of bread.

rules.rule: Yo and él share a form, so the subject is often named

examples.es: Yo trabajaba de noche y ella trabajaba de día.
examples.en: I worked nights and she worked days.

rules.rule: Stems don't change

examples.en: I wanted to go, but I couldn't.

rules.rule: Ser: era, eras, era, éramos, eran
Ir: iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, iban

examples.es: Iba a la playa cada verano.
examples.en: I went to the beach every summer.

rules.rule: Ver: veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veían
Habits, what used to happen

examples.es: De niño, jugaba en la calle.
examples.en: As a kid, I used to play in the street.

rules.rule: Descriptions: people, places, weather, time and age
What was going on when something happened

examples.en: I was reading when the phone rang.

rules.rule: Feelings and states of mind

examples.en: I didn't know what to do.

rules.rule: Siempre, todos los días, a menudo, de niño, mientras

examples.es: Todos los días tomábamos el bus.
examples.en: We took the bus every day.
While I cooked, I listened to music.

rules.note: Choosing between it and the preterite has a guide of its own.

title: Preterite vs. imperfect
summary: The preterite reports completed events. The imperfect sets the scene and describes what used to happen or was going on.

rules.rule: Completed actions

examples.en: Yesterday I ate chicken and rice.

rules.rule: A defined period of time, however long

examples.en: I lived in Cuba for twenty years.

rules.rule: A series of events that move a story forward

examples.es: Llegué, abrí la puerta y entré.
examples.en: I arrived, opened the door and went in.

rules.rule: Sudden changes or interruptions

examples.es: De repente se fue la luz.

rules.rule: Habits: used to, would

examples.es: De niño jugaba en la calle.
examples.en: As a child I used to play in the street.

rules.rule: Description and background

examples.es: Hacía sol y la playa estaba llena.
examples.en: It was sunny and the beach was full.

rules.rule: Actions in progress in the past

examples.en: I was cooking while she was reading.

rules.rule: Time and age in the past
The imperfect is the background, and the preterite is what happened

examples.en: I was sleeping when the phone rang.
It was raining when we left.

rules.rule: Conocer: met in the preterite, knew in the imperfect

examples.es: Conocí a mi esposa en un baile.
examples.en: I met my wife at a dance.

rules.rule: Saber: found out in the preterite, knew in the imperfect

examples.en: I found out the news yesterday.

rules.rule: Poder: managed to in the preterite, was able to in the imperfect
Querer: tried to in the preterite, wanted to in the imperfect
No querer in the preterite means refused

title: When to use the subjunctive
summary: The indicative states facts. The subjunctive covers what is wanted, felt, doubted or not yet real, usually after que with a change of subject.

rules.rule: A trigger in the main clause, then que, then a new subject
rules.note: With no change of subject, use the infinitive: Quiero venir.

rules.rule: Wishes and requests

examples.es: Espero que tengas un buen viaje.
examples.en: I hope you have a good trip.
I'm asking you to help me.

rules.rule: Emotions
Doubt and denial

examples.en: I doubt he'll arrive on time.

rules.note: Creo que takes the indicative: Creo que es verdad.

rules.rule: Judgments with es + adjective
rules.note: Facts take the indicative: Es verdad que viene.

rules.rule: Time words, when the event hasn't happened yet

examples.en: I'll wait for you until you finish.

rules.note: For habits or past facts, use the indicative: Cuando llego, te llamo.

rules.rule: Purpose and conditions: para que, a menos que, sin que, antes de que

examples.es: Hablo despacio para que me entiendas.
examples.en: I speak slowly so you'll understand me.

rules.note: Antes de que always takes the subjunctive.

rules.rule: Looking for something that may not exist

examples.es: Busco un apartamento que tenga balcón.
examples.en: I'm looking for an apartment that has a balcony.

examples.es: No hay nadie que sepa eso.

rules.note: A known one takes the indicative: Tengo un apartamento que tiene balcón.

rules.rule: The same triggers, in the past
Unreal conditions: si + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional

examples.en: If I had money, I would travel.

rules.note: Never use the present subjunctive after si.

rules.rule: Polite requests

title: The imperfect subjunctive and si clauses
summary: The imperfect subjunctive is the subjunctive in the past, and the way to talk about what isn't true. It's built from the ellos form of the preterite.

rules.rule: Take the ellos preterite, drop -ron, and add -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -ran

examples.en: I wanted you to talk to me.
She asked me to eat something.

rules.note: Nosotros takes a written accent: habláramos, comiéramos.

rules.rule: Irregular preterites carry over

examples.en: If I had time, I'd go.

examples.es: Le pedí que me dijera la verdad.
examples.en: I asked him to tell me the truth.
I wish I could help you.

rules.note: Tuvieron gives tuviera, dijeron gives dijera, and fueron gives fuera for both ser and ir.

rules.rule: The -se forms mean the same

examples.en: If I had time, I'd go.

rules.note: The -ra forms are far more common in Latin American speech, and they're what the drills ask for.

sections.heading: The same triggers, in the past

rules.rule: A wish, feeling or doubt in the past takes the imperfect subjunctive

examples.es: Quiero que vengas. Quería que vinieras.
examples.en: I want you to come. I wanted you to come.
I didn't think it was true.

examples.es: Te lo expliqué para que entendieras.
examples.en: I explained it so you'd understand.

rules.rule: Not true or unlikely: si plus the imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional

examples.en: If I had money, I'd travel.

examples.es: Si fuera más joven, estudiaría medicina.
examples.en: If I were younger, I'd study medicine.

examples.es: Viviría en la playa si pudiera.
examples.en: I'd live at the beach if I could.

rules.note: The conditional never comes right after si: si tuviera, not si tendría.

rules.rule: Likely: si plus the present, then the present or future

examples.en: If it rains, I'm not going out.
If I have time, I'll call you.

rules.rule: Como si always takes it

examples.es: Habla como si fuera el jefe.
examples.en: He talks as if he were the boss.

rules.rule: Ojalá plus the imperfect subjunctive, for wishes that probably won't come true

examples.en: I wish I had more time.

rules.rule: Quisiera, for a polite I'd like

title: Noun gender and plurals
summary: Every noun is masculine or feminine. The ending usually tells you which, and plurals follow a few simple rules.

rules.rule: Most nouns ending in -o
Days, months, seas, rivers and numbers
Most nouns ending in -aje, -or, or -án
Most nouns ending in -a
Nouns ending in -ción, -sión, -dad, -tad, -tud or -umbre
Masculine nouns ending in -a, many from Greek and ending in -ma
Feminine nouns ending in -o
rules.note: Foto and moto are short for fotografía and motocicleta.

rules.rule: Feminine nouns starting with a stressed a take el in the singular
rules.note: They stay feminine, so adjectives agree in the feminine.

rules.rule: Same word, different meaning
Words ending in -e or a consonant have to be learned one by one
Ending in a vowel: add -s
Ending in a consonant: add -es
Ending in -z: change it to -ces
Unstressed final -s: no change
Accents shift to keep the stress in place
A mixed group takes the masculine plural

title: Reflexive verbs
summary: A reflexive verb uses a pronoun that points back at the subject. It often shows someone acting on themselves, but it can also change a verb's meaning.

rules.rule: Me, te, se, nos, and se for ellos and ustedes
Before a conjugated verb
Before the whole verb in perfect tenses
Attached to an infinitive or gerund, or before the verb in front of it
rules.note: Attaching it to a gerund often needs a written accent.

rules.rule: Attached to an affirmative command
Daily routine
Each other, with plural subjects

examples.en: We hugged each other at the airport.

rules.rule: Becoming or changing state
Body parts and clothing take the, not my
Ir to go, irse to leave
Dormir to sleep, dormirse to fall asleep

examples.en: I fell asleep at the movies.

rules.rule: Poner to put, ponerse to put on or become
Llamar to call, llamarse to be named
Acordar to agree, acordarse to remember
Parecer to seem, parecerse a to look like
Impersonal: people in general, or no specific person
Accidents: the thing happens to you
rules.note: This takes the blame off the person, and it's very common in everyday speech.

title: Object pronouns
summary: Object pronouns replace the thing or person a verb acts on. Direct objects answer what or whom; indirect objects answer to whom or for whom.

rules.rule: Direct objects: me, te, lo, la, nos, los, las

examples.en: I bought the book. I bought it.
I see María. I see her.

rules.rule: Indirect objects: me, te, le, nos, les

examples.es: Le di dinero a mi hijo.

rules.note: Latin American Spanish uses lo for a male direct object. Le for him is mainly heard in Spain.

rules.rule: Usted and ustedes use the third-person pronouns

examples.en: I'll bring you all the check.

rules.rule: Before a conjugated verb
Attached to an infinitive or gerund, or before the verb in front of it
Attached to affirmative commands, before negative ones
Indirect comes before direct

examples.en: I'll send it to you tomorrow.

rules.rule: Le and les change to se before lo, la, los, las
rules.note: Never le lo. Add a él or a ella if it isn't clear who se means.

rules.rule: Attaching two pronouns usually needs a written accent

examples.en: I want to give it to you.

rules.rule: The personal a comes before a direct object that's a specific person
The indirect pronoun stays even when the person is named

examples.es: Le di el libro a Juan.
examples.en: I gave the book to Juan.

rules.rule: Gustar works backward: the thing liked is the subject

examples.es: A mi madre le gusta bailar.

rules.note: Doler, encantar and faltar work the same way.

rules.rule: A + pronoun adds emphasis or clarity

examples.es: A mí me gusta, pero a él no.
examples.en: I like it, but he doesn't.

title: Commands
summary: Commands change with who you're talking to and whether you're telling them to do something or not to.

rules.rule: Affirmative: use the él form of the present
Negative: no + present subjunctive
Eight verbs have short affirmative forms: di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven
rules.note: Their negatives are regular subjunctives: no digas, no hagas, no vayas, no pongas, no salgas, no seas, no tengas, no vengas.

rules.rule: Both affirmative and negative use the present subjunctive
Ustedes is the plural for everyone in Latin America
rules.note: Spain uses vosotros for friends and family, which you can skip for Latin American Spanish.

rules.rule: Use the present subjunctive
Vamos a + infinitive is more common in speech
Ir uses vamos, and vámonos with a pronoun
The final -s drops before nos
Pronouns attach to affirmative commands, often adding a written accent
Pronouns go before negative commands
Questions in the present are a natural, polite way to ask

examples.en: Can you pass me the salt?

rules.rule: Por favor softens any command

title: The perfect tenses
summary: Perfect tenses combine a form of haber with a past participle to talk about something completed before another point in time.

rules.rule: Conjugate haber, and the participle never changes
Regular participles end in -ado or -ido
Common irregular participles
Nothing goes between haber and the participle
rules.note: Pronouns, no and adverbs go before haber.

rules.rule: Present perfect, has or have done
Pluperfect, also called the past perfect: had done

examples.en: I had already eaten when you arrived.

rules.rule: Future perfect, will have done

examples.en: By June I will have finished.

rules.rule: Conditional perfect, would have done

examples.en: I would have gone with you.

rules.rule: Present perfect subjunctive, after subjunctive triggers
Pluperfect subjunctive, also called the past perfect subjunctive, for what didn't happen
Latin America usually prefers the preterite for recent events
rules.note: In Spain you'd often hear ¿Ya has comido? and Hoy me he levantado temprano.

rules.rule: The present perfect is natural for life experience
It's also used for things continuing up to now
Si + pluperfect subjunctive, then the conditional perfect

examples.en: If I had studied, I would have passed.

rules.rule: The conditional also works for a present result

examples.es: Si hubiera estudiado, ahora tendría trabajo.
examples.en: If I had studied, I would have a job now.

rules.rule: With estar the participle acts as an adjective and agrees
Acabar de + infinitive means have just
Hay is not a perfect tense, but its perfect is ha habido

title: Comparisons
summary: Use más, menos and tan to compare people and things, and a few irregular words for good, bad, old and young.

rules.rule: Más + adjective + que

examples.es: Mi hermano es más alto que yo.
examples.en: My brother is taller than me.

rules.rule: Menos + adjective + que

examples.es: Este carro es menos caro que el otro.
examples.en: This car is less expensive than the other one.

rules.rule: It also works with nouns, verbs and adverbs

examples.en: I have more work than you.
She runs more than I do.
I arrived later than he did.

rules.rule: Use de, not que, before a number

examples.en: I have more than twenty cousins.
It costs less than ten dollars.

rules.note: In a negative sentence, no más que means only: No tengo más que diez dólares.

rules.rule: Tan + adjective or adverb + como

examples.es: Ana es tan alta como su madre.
examples.en: Ana is as tall as her mother.
You speak as fast as I do.

rules.rule: Tanto + noun + como, agreeing with the noun

examples.es: No tengo tanto dinero como tú.
examples.en: I don't have as much money as you.

examples.es: No tengo tantas camisas como él.
examples.en: I don't have as many shirts as he does.

rules.rule: Verb + tanto como, with no agreement

examples.en: I don't work as much as before.

rules.rule: Igual de + adjective + que is common in speech

examples.es: Es igual de caro que el otro.
examples.en: It's just as expensive as the other one.

rules.rule: Bueno becomes mejor, and malo becomes peor

examples.es: Este café es mejor que ese.
examples.en: This coffee is better than that one.

rules.note: Never más bueno for quality in careful speech. Mejor and peor add -es in the plural.

rules.rule: Mayor and menor for age

examples.es: Mi hermana mayor vive en Ponce.
examples.en: My older sister lives in Ponce.

rules.rule: Bien becomes mejor, and mal becomes peor, as adverbs

examples.en: I slept worse than last night.

rules.rule: El, la, los or las + más + adjective + de

examples.es: Es la playa más bonita de la isla.
examples.en: It's the prettiest beach on the island.

examples.es: Es el más alto de la familia.
examples.en: He's the tallest in the family.

rules.note: Use de for in, never en.

rules.rule: With mejor and peor, no más is needed

examples.es: Es el mejor restaurante de la ciudad.
examples.en: It's the best restaurant in the city.

rules.rule: Add -ísimo for very, very
rules.note: The word drops its final vowel first, and spelling can change: rico, riquísimo.

title: Talking about the future
summary: Everyday speech mostly uses ir a + infinitive. The simple future is for promises, formal plans and guesses.

rules.rule: Conjugate ir, add a, then the infinitive

examples.en: We're going to travel in May.

rules.rule: It's the normal choice in conversation

examples.es: Mañana voy a ir al mercado.
examples.en: Tomorrow I'm going to go to the market.

rules.rule: Pronouns go before ir or attach to the infinitive
Hay becomes va a haber

examples.en: There's going to be a party.

rules.note: It stays singular: Va a haber muchas personas.

rules.rule: Use the present for plans and schedules, with a time word

examples.es: El vuelo sale a las ocho.

rules.rule: Offers and suggestions also use the present
Promises and strong intentions
News, forecasts and formal plans

examples.es: Mañana lloverá en toda la isla.
examples.en: It will rain across the whole island tomorrow.

rules.rule: Guessing about the present

examples.en: I wonder what time it is.

rules.note: This use has nothing to do with the future.

rules.rule: After cuando and similar words, a future event takes the subjunctive, not the future

examples.en: I'll call you when I arrive.
I'm going to eat when I finish.

rules.note: Cuando llegaré is a common learner mistake.

rules.rule: Iba a + infinitive: was going to

examples.es: Iba a llamarte, pero se me olvidó.
examples.en: I was going to call you, but I forgot.

rules.rule: The conditional reports what someone said would happen

title: Relative pronouns
summary: Relative pronouns link a description to a noun, like who, that and which in English. In Spanish, que does most of the work.

rules.rule: Use que for people and things

examples.es: El hombre que vive aquí es mi tío.
examples.en: The man who lives here is my uncle.

examples.es: El libro que leí es muy bueno.
examples.en: The book that I read is very good.

rules.rule: It can't be left out, even when English drops that
Use them for people after a preposition

examples.es: La mujer con quien hablé es médica.
examples.en: The woman I spoke with is a doctor.

examples.es: Los amigos a quienes invité no vinieron.
examples.en: The friends I invited didn't come.

rules.note: Quien isn't used as a plain who in the middle of a sentence: el hombre que vive aquí, not el hombre quien vive aquí.

rules.rule: It can mean whoever or the one who
They agree with the noun, and work after prepositions

examples.es: La casa en la que vivo es pequeña.
examples.en: The house I live in is small.

examples.es: El carro con el que viajamos es viejo.
examples.en: The car we traveled in is old.

rules.note: The preposition goes before the pronoun, never at the end of the sentence as in English.

rules.rule: They can also mean the one that or those who

examples.es: Mi camisa es la que está ahí.
examples.en: My shirt is the one over there.
Those who want to can come.

rules.rule: Use lo que for what, in the sense of the thing that

examples.en: I don't understand what you're saying.
What I want is to rest.

rules.note: Use qué only in questions: ¿Qué dices?

rules.rule: It can refer to a whole idea, like which in English

examples.es: Llegó tarde, lo que me molestó.
examples.en: He arrived late, which bothered me.

rules.rule: Donde for places

examples.es: Este es el barrio donde crecí.
examples.en: This is the neighborhood where I grew up.

rules.rule: Cuando for times

examples.es: Fue en mayo cuando nos conocimos.
examples.en: It was in May when we met.

rules.rule: Cuyo means whose, and agrees with what's owned

examples.en: The woman whose house we bought.

examples.es: El hombre cuyos hijos viven aquí.
examples.en: The man whose children live here.

rules.note: This is mainly written Spanish. In speech, people usually rephrase.

rules.rule: Question words take an accent, relatives don't

examples.en: I don't know what you want.

rules.note: Indirect questions keep the accent, as in the last example.

title: Numbers, dates and time
summary: How to say numbers, dates, times and ages, including the small rules that catch people out.

rules.rule: 16 to 29 are written as one word
rules.note: Several take an accent: dieciséis, veintidós, veintitrés, veintiséis.

rules.rule: From 31 on, use tens + y + ones

examples.es: treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco

rules.rule: Uno shortens before a masculine noun and changes before a feminine one
Cien alone or before a noun, ciento in combinations
rules.note: Never un cien.

rules.rule: Hundreds agree with feminine nouns
Watch the irregular hundreds
Mil has no un, and doesn't go plural in counting
Millón takes un and de
First through tenth agree with the noun
rules.note: The series is primero, segundo, tercero, cuarto, quinto, sexto, séptimo, octavo, noveno, décimo.

rules.rule: Primero and tercero shorten before a masculine singular noun
Days and months aren't capitalized
El means on with days, and los means every
Dates are el + number + de + month

examples.es: Hoy es el cinco de mayo.
Nací el diez de junio de 1990.

rules.note: Written dates put the day first, so 5/6 is June 5th.

rules.rule: Latin America uses primero for the first of the month
rules.note: Spain usually says el uno de enero.

rules.rule: Years are read as whole numbers
Es la una, and son las for everything else
Add minutes with y
Before the hour, Latin America often uses faltan or para
Use a la or a las for at

examples.es: La clase es a las nueve.

rules.rule: Parts of the day use de with a clock time, por without

examples.es: Son las ocho de la mañana.

rules.rule: Use tener, not ser
rules.note: Keep the ñ in años. Without it, the word is something very different.

title: Idioms and everyday expressions
summary: Fixed expressions that don't translate word for word, from tener hambre to meter la pata, and the sayings people quote every day.

rules.rule: Hunger, thirst, sleepiness, cold, heat, fear and hurry
rules.note: These are nouns, so very is mucho or mucha: tengo mucha hambre.

rules.rule: Tener razón: to be right
Tener ganas de: to feel like
Hacer falta: to be needed
Darse cuenta: to realize
Me da igual, me da miedo, me da pena
rules.note: Like gustar, the thing is the subject, so it's dan for more than one.

rules.rule: Valer la pena: to be worth it
Llevarse bien or mal: to get along, or not

examples.es: Me llevo bien con mi suegra.
examples.en: I get along well with my mother-in-law.

rules.rule: Estar de acuerdo: to agree
Extrañar: to miss someone or something
rules.note: Echar de menos is understood everywhere, but most of Latin America says extrañar.

rules.rule: Meter la pata: to put your foot in it
Tomar el pelo: to pull someone's leg
Costar un ojo de la cara: to cost an arm and a leg

examples.es: Ese carro cuesta un ojo de la cara.
examples.en: That car costs an arm and a leg.

rules.rule: Ponerse las pilas: to get your act together

examples.es: Ponte las pilas, que el examen es mañana.
examples.en: Get it together, the exam is tomorrow.

rules.rule: Se, then me, te or le, then the verb, for accidents
rules.note: The thing is the subject, so it's plural with more than one: se me olvidaron las llaves.

rules.rule: ¡Qué! plus a noun or adjective
Surprise and refusal

examples.en: No way, out of the question!

rules.rule: Ni modo: oh well
rules.note: Common in Mexico and Central America.

rules.rule: Refranes come up all the time, often only the first half

examples.en: Keep your chin up in hard times.

examples.es: Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente.

rules.note: Saying camarón que se duerme is enough, since everyone knows the rest.
